seal.statement: Zero ambient clock reads from simulator-hosted production code. Production time is supplied solely by the owning node or subsystem TimeSource, threaded from the owner that already holds one rather than minted locally, and the one deterministic-owner ambient-seam guard covers every tagged production execution boundary - scheduler dispatch as well as owner-pass execution - so the next missed seam refuses instead of hiding. The acceptance condition is the dynamic one: in a deterministic run, ambient clock reads and ambient timer scheduling from tagged production are both zero for the APIs the guard owns.

text: First owner slice landed and the classification is confirmed end to end. ReplicaOperationRepository now takes timeSource as a construction dependency through the standard resolveTimeSource default, RebalanceCoordinator threads its own clock down rather than letting a second one be minted, and all 23 ambient reads across the repository's six method modules became this.timeSource.now(). The falsifier is pinned on the exact branch the divergence was traced to: with a virtual owner clock parked below nextIncompleteOperationSqlRetryAtMs no authoritative read happens, advancing the owner clock across the deadline admits it, and swapping the repository's clock back to the ambient one makes that witness red. Separately the guard's boundary was wrong in a way worth recording: coverage was not missing at scheduler dispatch, it was TIME-SLICED. guardedDispatch swapped the globals, called the body and restored them in finally, but every dispatch body is async, so the guard was gone before a single continuation ran - which is how a proven guard and 812 ambient reads coexisted. The replacements are now installed once and decide per async context through AsyncLocalStorage, so they survive an await; one authority, unchanged vocabulary, wider boundary. Result: cold run 1 now equals warm runs 2 and 3 exactly, 296 identical metered entries, and attribution witness A is green. Remaining ambient surface fell from 21 sites / 332 reads inside tagged execution to 17 / 165, and from 26 / 539 outside to 19 / 241.

Two results that change the plan, both measured. First, a guard that throws is not a reliable seam detector here: with the widened boundary the scenario still completes rather than refusing, because production catches the refusal as an ordinary error and degrades. 165 ambient reads across 17 production sites currently fall inside tagged execution and are each being swallowed, so guard-driven migration cannot simply be 'run until it refuses' - the refusals have to be counted rather than awaited. Second, the tagging boundary has a hole one level up: 241 reads across 19 sites happen in production code running OUTSIDE any tagged context, largely continuations released by the harness's own owner-idle awaits, which are production execution but run in harness async context. Also recorded: the planner completion contract's mutation witness can no longer falsify. It falsified while the ambient-clock escape was open - neutering the contract made run 1 disagree with later runs, 45 planning reads against 51 - but with owner-owned production time the same mutation moves nothing, 9 reads per run either way and none after return, because the scenario no longer performs the redundant work the leak showed up in. The witness was removed rather than weakened; the contract now rests on its causal argument alone.

Slice 2 landed and the tagging census is corrected. The guard now records every ambient access before throwing it, with generation-scoped count, per-primitive tallies and bounded samples carrying owner, execution node and first callsite; assertNoNondeterministicOwnerSeam refuses a run with a non-zero count. T3 is the falsifier that matters: a tagged dispatch that catches its own Date.now() refusal and returns normally still refuses the deterministic proof. On a real scenario the ledger reports 19 ambient accesses, all Date.now, first sites cdc-integration-service-mutation-operations.js:424, authoritative-node-evidence-reconciler.js:525, cdc-integration-service-authoritative-catchup.js:198, rebalancer-priority-recovery-planning-gate-methods.js:699 and logging-service.js:278. Note that 19 is the count under a guard that throws, and production degrades when it does, so the run being counted is not the run being certified until the count reaches zero. Correction to my previous report, which was wrong: the untagged production execution is NOT harness construction. My first probe read a non-exported accessor and silently reported null for every node, so everything looked off-node. With currentFormationExecutionNodeId the split is 240 of 241 untagged reads executing ON a simulated node and exactly 1 off-node (logging init). So the owner's context-lineage hypothesis holds: production execution carries the node frame while the guard's production tag is absent. The two tags are separate authorities that disagree - runOnExecutionNode propagates the node, guardedDispatch propagates the production tag, and construction, seeding and released continuations get one without the other.

Slice 1 authority cutover landed. currentFormationExecutionContext() reads the SAME async-local record runOnExecutionNode writes and returns {generationId, executionNodeId} RAW - the generation travels with the frame rather than being looked up from a module global, which is what stops one generation from donating node identity to the next. The guard's admission predicate is now that context alone: generation present and execution node present. guardedDispatch no longer establishes production identity; it installs the wrappers and names the owner for violation records only, and owner is diagnostics - an unattributed segment is refused exactly like a named one. Nine witnesses green: L1 raw ambient read while executing as a node, with no dispatch involved; L2 the authority surviving a promise continuation, attributed to the same generation and node; L3 production resumed behind a neutral harness idle wait still refused while the harness continuation after the await stays neutral; L4 owner-null production still refused; L5 harness at the generation root keeping real host time and recording nothing; L6 a detached generation-A continuation resuming during generation B still naming A; the retired-predicate mutation; and T3/T4 from slice 2. The truthful list the cutover exposed is much larger than the old one: 405 ambient Date.now accesses inside simulated-node execution in one scenario, led by system-table-cache.js:502 with 106, priority-recovery-observation.js:351 with 45, move-planner-state-methods.js:406 and unified-rebalancer-rebalance-loop.js:390 with 30 each, then the topology-guard, owner-delegation, CDC mutation and authoritative-catchup sites. The old 165/240 split is obsolete as predicted.

Discovery mode and the completion structural falsifier landed; the deadlock is resolved without host time entering the scenario. Strict stays the default and is unchanged: record, throw, and a terminal ledger assertion that must also be zero. Discovery records the violation and then, for Date.now only, returns the clock the simulated node ALREADY owns, resolved through the simulator composition's own network.networkTimeSource(nodeId) - the guard constructs nothing, the execution context stays pure identity, and if no node clock can be resolved the strict refusal stands. Timers, performance.now and every other forbidden intrinsic still record and throw, because none has an equally unambiguous substitute. Proof eligibility is structural rather than conventional: every report now carries proofEligibility, and a discovery run or any run with a non-zero ledger is deterministicProofEligible false. A discovery scenario completes with 405 violations and 405 substitutions, and cold run 1 equals warm runs 2 and 3 exactly at 391 metered entries, so the migration-observation lane works while defects remain. The completion contract now has a permanent structural proof that needs no scenario and no AVAILABLE-read traffic: a real OwnerKeyReconcileQueue admits work at virtual T, the reconcile crosses a pure promise continuation and only then records its effect, and closeCurrentInstant is asked to close T. With the owner in the closure set the effect lands at T; with the owner omitted the instant closes first, the effect is still owed, and it arrives afterwards. Structural lane green at 450.

Formation design amended before the first owner edit, so a later agent cannot revert these contracts by not knowing them: execution authority is the generation plus execution-node context alone, propagating through async lineage with the generation travelling on the frame; violation recording is generation-scoped and happens before any handling, so a caught exception cannot neutralise it; strict is record, throw and terminal zero; discover records and substitutes only the node's own Date.now, is structurally proof-ineligible, and never consumes host time; owner current-work completion participates in current-instant causal closure; and no valid metered oracle exists, with every number measured during migration named as transient.

Four owner slices migrated by strict first-refusal order, not by census rank. SystemTableCache took one optional TimeSource for its mutation watermark, with RealTimeSource still the default and the simulated node supplying its own clock; the _cacheId stayed diagnostic identity and became injectable rather than a clock consumer, so a debug string is not a reason to read host time inside a node. CDCIntegrationService was constructing HLCClockService without threading its clock, so the HLC defaulted to RealTimeSource inside a simulated node - that was the time-source.js:41 violation, and the repair was the missing arrow at the construction boundary, not any change to RealTimeSource. The seeding row builder createNodeEntry now receives nowMs as data with an ambient default, so harness seeding on a node frame stamps node time. The CDC mutation and routed-readiness paths were violating an already-established owner clock and now read this.timeSource.now(). Strict now runs to completion, which is not yet proof: the ledger records 44 and deterministicProofEligible is false, because production catches the refusals and degrades. That is precisely the case the ledger exists for, and it is not a substrate bug. Counts moved 34 to 40 to 44 across slices, as expected when a repair changes the legal path.

First genuine contract collision in the migration, recorded rather than resolved. Routing the authoritative catch-up sweep's readStartedAtMs to the service clock broke a sealed witness that deliberately keeps it ambient: cdc-integration-service-time-seam.test.js pins that the stamp is compared against row updated_at and tombstone times stamped by their WRITERS, and seaming it alone leaves the sweep inert - the verifier measured rowsSwept 0 against 1 in round 3. So that stamp cannot move to owner time before the writers of those row timestamps do. I reverted it and left the reasoning in the source next to the read, so it reads as a known open ambient site on the hosted path rather than an oversight. It is now 4 of the 44 remaining violations. Remaining owners by sample: rebalancer-priority-recovery-planning-gate-methods.js:699 at 12, logging-service.js:278 at 12, authoritative-node-evidence-reconciler.js:525 at 4, and that catch-up stamp at 4.

Slices closed and the remaining owners migrated by strict first-refusal order; the ledger fell 44 to 6. Witnesses first: the cache now has a timestamp-source witness proving the watermark is stamped at the injected clock's instant, moves with it, keeps RealTimeSource and an ambient instance id by default, and goes red when the clock is swapped to ambient - and writing that witness found a second watermark write in the authoritative-absence sweep, now on the same cache clock. CDC has a threading witness proving the HLC reads its parent's clock, that its physical component tracks the owner across an advance, and that a defaulted HLC starts on platform time, which is the drift the threading removed. Then: the reconciler's repair cause id moved to its existing this.now(); the planning-gate diagnostic to the rebalancer's nowFn; the workflow owner's two priority-recovery observation stamps to resolveTimeoutCheckNowMs; the move planner to a projection of the rebalancer's clock rather than a clock of its own; the rebalance loop and the coordinator's owner-delegation stamps to their owners. The largest single leverage was a dual-authority defect rather than a missing seam: RebalanceCoordinator.nowFn defaulted to Date.now even when the coordinator had been handed a TimeSource, so every nowFn caller read host time underneath an owner that thought it was seamed. Projecting nowFn from this.timeSource took the ledger from 40 to 6 and removed the logging sites with it. Suites green: rebalancer 6792, control-plane 8891, cache and CDC 2230. Discover cold equals warm exactly at 391 across three same-process runs.

Terminal clock closure reached. Stage 1 first: the CDC write path got a duration witness in the shape the timestamp actually owns rather than an invented threshold - virtual time advances by 4000 ms inside a controlled dependency and the reported sqlDurationMs is exactly that, while the cache wait, which consumed no virtual time, reports none; the mutation puts one end of the duration on ambient time and the end-to-end claim breaks. Stage 2 then did the domain in the prescribed order. SystemTableCacheTombstoneStore takes its parent cache's TimeSource rather than resolving one, covering deletedAtMs, prune, expiry and complete-observation fencing, with a TTL witness proving a tombstone is alive at the boundary and expired one virtual millisecond later, fencing following the same clock through record and prune, an ambient mutation leaving the comparison domain, and the default store still on platform time. Only then the consumer moved: the catch-up readStartedAtMs now reads the CDC owner's clock. The sealed witness keeps its expectation - rowsSwept 1, the same intended scenario - and passes again once its row is stamped in the same domain as the reader, which is the proof that the consumer was never wrong and the domain was incomplete. Its red-on-revert is a producer mutation: put the ROW's stamp back on the process clock and the sweep goes inert at rowsSwept 0 exactly as it did when only the consumer had moved. Strict now reports 0 violations, 0 substitutions, deterministicProofEligible true; discover on the same seed reports 0 and 0; and the two reports are byte-identical. The old runner guard witness was rewritten onto the new authority rather than deleted.
